fixes.explanation: A king is a natural guess when a heavy load shows up, friend. But no king appears in this verse, and the writer looks higher than any throne. He says, “…for the LORD has laid it upon him.” A few verses later he says the Lord will not cast us off forever, and I think that's what keeps this line from being the last word.

Yes, friend. “Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.” Grief is real in this poem, and the writer says so out loud. But compassion follows right in the same verse, tied to His abundant loving devotion.

Yes. “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?” I once told a hot batch to cool faster, and that batch ignored me completely. The writer's answer is right in the question: the Lord. Nobody else in the verse gets that credit.

A king of Babylon is a natural guess, friend, since kings are the ones we picture giving orders. But no king is named in this verse. The writer asks, “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?” He puts the Lord above every speaker, and the very next verse says both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High.
